title: Sound and Silence
sub: Grades 5–8 · Music · How the exhibition remembers with sound, and without it

hero.credit: Ted Eytan, *Holocaust Day*. CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

objective: Students will listen to the few quiet sounds the exhibition uses — a candle lit, a far-off bell, water, steps on iron — and map where it chooses **silence** instead: no music under the posters, a film whose music stops on the words *“Six million Jews had been murdered.”*, and a minute’s stillness with no sound at all. They will describe sounds by **dynamics, duration and timbre**, and compose a one-minute **graphic score** in which silence is part of the music.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Silence is not empty. Keeping silence together is one of the oldest ways people remember, and composers use it as carefully as any note.

items.text: describe a short sound by its dynamics, duration and timbre, and say what it brings to mind

materials: Speakers; the clips on the classroom screen; *The sounds in this lesson* on page 3
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** turn the sound on and read the two posters; watch the film and walk the iron with your steps; then keep *A Minute’s Stillness*, which has no sound at all.

steps.title: What do you hear?
script: Play the three sounds without naming them. *“Listen twice, eyes closed. What do you hear? Where might you be?”* Take answers. Then: these are the only sounds on the exhibition’s two posters — a match lighting a candle, a church bell far off, water lapping. Each is played once, very quietly, as its panel arrives. **There is no music under the posters.**

screen.question: Listen to each sound twice, with your eyes closed. What do you hear? Where might you be?

steps.purpose: Listen before knowing: let each sound suggest its own picture.
students: What do you hear in each?
Is it loud or soft? Long or short?

steps.title: A sound map
script: Build the sound map together (page 3). On the timeline, most stops are silent; three sound, each a moment already heard on the posters — a candle for the Warsaw ghetto uprising, which began on the eve of Passover; the sea for the Normandy beaches; a bell for the end of the war in Europe. In *A Minute’s Stillness* there is no sound at all.

steps.purpose: See that the exhibition chooses sound rarely, and silence often.
students: Where is there none? Why there?

steps.title: Steps on iron
script: Play one step and the rattle. Read the exhibition’s words about its Walk: *“As you walk, the iron sounds under your feet. It is the sound of those who died, crying up from below.”* Ask what a single, repeated, unaccompanied sound does.

screen.question: The floor is covered with iron faces, each one different, too many to count. They stand for the people who died in the Holocaust. As you walk, the iron sounds under your feet. It is the sound of those who died, crying up from below.

steps.purpose: Hear how a single, repeated sound can carry meaning.
students: Describe the step, and the rattle.

steps.title: Where the music stops
script: Explain that the Walk’s film has music, and that it **ends on the words** *“Six million Jews had been murdered.”* The lines after are in silence. Ask: *why stop there?*

screen.text: Six million Jews had been murdered.
screen.cite: The Walk’s film: its music ends on these words; the lines after them are in silence

steps.purpose: Think about what a silence says that music cannot.
students: Why might the music stop here?
What does the silence after it do?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. Every level ends with a one-minute graphic score that is at least half silence.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Describe the three moments (loud or soft, long or short, what they bring to mind), match each to its place on the posters, then fill in a six-box score with a symbol key.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Map where the exhibition uses sound and silence and explain one choice, then compose a three-layer score and write a 40–60 word program note.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Weigh the exhibition’s choices — steps without music, music that stops, a minute without sound — argue when silence remembers better than music, then compose and defend a score.

steps.purpose: Listen, explain and compose at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. Every level ends with a one-minute score.

steps.title: A minute’s stillness
script: Two groups perform their scores. Then, with no comment, keep **one minute of stillness** together, as the exhibition’s last room invites. Afterward ask: *was the minute empty?*

screen.question: Listen to two scores. Then keep one minute of stillness together.

steps.purpose: Hear silence as part of the music, then keep it together.
students: Then keep one minute of stillness together.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
